216: "All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad, the other is with the Guards, who are marching to the frontier. Our dear Emperor is leaving Petersburg and, it is supposed, intends himself to expose his precious existence to the chances of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is disturbing the peace of Europe may be brought low by the angel whom the Almighty in His goodness has set over us as our sovereign. Not to mention my brothers, this war has deprived me of one of the connections dearest to my heart. I speak of young Nikolai Rostov, who, with his enthusiasm, could not bear to remain idle and left the university to enter the army. I confess to you, dear Marie, that despite his extreme youth his departure for the army was a great grief to me. In the young man of whom I spoke to you last summer there is so much nobility, such true youthfulness as one so rarely meets in our day among our twenty-year-old graybeards! He has, above all, so much openness and warmth of heart. He is so pure and so full of poetry that my relations with him, fleeting as they were, were one of the sweetest comforts of my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. I shall tell you someday of our parting and all that was said at that parting. It is all still too fresh... Ah, dear friend, you are fortunate not to know these burning joys, these burning sorrows. You are fortunate, for the latter are commonly stronger than the former. I know very well that Count Nikolai is too young ever to become anything more to me than a friend. But this sweet friendship, these relations so poetic and so pure, were a need of my heart. But enough of this. The chief news occupying all Moscow is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Imagine, the three princesses received some trifle, Prince Vasili nothing, and Pierre is heir to everything and, moreover, has been recognized as the legitimate son and consequently Count Bezukhov and possessor of the largest fortune in Russia. They say that Prince Vasili played a very ugly part in the whole affair, and that he went off to Petersburg quite crestfallen. I confess I understand very little of all these matters of wills; I only know that since the young man whom we all knew simply as Pierre became Count Bezukhov and possessor of one of the finest fortunes in Russia, I have amused myself watching the change of tone among the mammas who have marriageable daughters, and among the young ladies themselves, toward this gentleman who (be it said in parenthesis) always struck me as a very insignificant person. As for two years now everyone has amused himself finding husbands for me, most of whom I do not even know, the marriage chronicle of Moscow now makes me Countess Bezukhova. But you understand that I have not the least desire for this. Speaking of marriages, do you know that our universal aunt Anna Mikhaylovna confided to me lately, under the greatest secrecy, a scheme for arranging your marriage? It is nothing less than Prince Vasili's son, Anatole, whom they wish to settle by marrying him to some rich and well-born young lady, and the choice of the parents has fallen upon you. I do not know how you will look upon the matter, but I felt it my duty to forewarn you. He is said to be very handsome and a great rake; that is all I have been able to learn about him. But enough of gossip. I am finishing my second sheet, and mamma has sent for me to go and dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I am sending you; it has a tremendous success with us. Though there are things in it hard for the feeble human mind to grasp, it is an excellent book; reading it calms and elevates the soul. Farewell. My respects to your father, and my compliments to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you with all my heart. Julie. P.S. Let me know about your brother and his charming wife."
217: "Dear and precious friend. Your letter of the 13th gave me great joy. So you still love me, my poetic Julie. Separation, of which you speak so ill, has evidently not had its usual effect upon you. You complain of separation — what, then, should I say, if I dared, I who am deprived of all who are dear to me? Ah, were it not for the consolation of religion, life would be very sad. Why do you attribute to me a stern view when you speak of your inclination toward the young man? On this point I am strict only with myself. I understand such feelings in others, and if, never having experienced them, I cannot approve of them, neither do I condemn them. It only seems to me that Christian love for one's neighbor, love for one's enemies, is more worthy, more comforting, and better than the feelings that a young man's fine eyes can inspire in a poetic and loving young girl like you. The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was greatly moved by it. He says that the count was the last but one of the great generation, and that now it is his own turn, but that he will do everything in his power to see that his turn comes as late as possible. God preserve us from that misfortune! I cannot share your opinion of Pierre, whom I knew as a child. It always seemed to me that he had an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and the part Prince Vasili played in it, it is very sad for them both. Ah, dear friend, the words of our Divine Saviour, that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, are terribly true! I pity Prince Vasili, and still more Pierre. That one so young should be burdened with so vast a fortune — through how many temptations will he have to pass! If I were asked what I desire most in the world, I should say: I desire to be poorer than the poorest of beggars. Thank you a thousand times, dear friend, for the book you are sending me, which is making such a stir among you. However, since you tell me that among many good things it contains some that the feeble human mind cannot grasp, it seems to me useless to occupy oneself with reading that cannot be understood, which for that very reason could bring no benefit. I have never been able to understand the passion that certain persons have for confusing their minds by attaching themselves to mystical books, which only arouse doubts in their minds, excite their imagination, and give them a tendency to exaggeration wholly contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us rather read the Apostles and the Gospel. Let us not try to penetrate what is mysterious in those books, for how can we, wretched sinners that we are, know the terrible and sacred secrets of Providence while we still bear that fleshly covering which raises an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us rather confine ourselves to studying the great rules which our Divine Saviour has left us for our guidance here on earth; let us try to follow them, and let us try to convince ourselves that the less freedom we give to our minds, the more pleasing we shall be to God, Who rejects all knowledge that does not come from Him, and that the less we probe into what He has been pleased to hide from us, the sooner will He grant us that revelation through His divine wisdom. My father has said nothing to me about a suitor, but told me only that he had received a letter and was expecting a visit from Prince Vasili; as for the marriage plan concerning myself, I will tell you, dear and precious friend, that marriage, in my opinion, is a divine institution to which one must submit. However hard it may be for me, if it should please the Almighty to lay upon me the duties of wife and mother, I shall try to fulfil them as faithfully as I can, without troubling myself to examine my feelings toward him whom He gives me for a husband. I have had a letter from my brother, announcing his coming to Bald Hills with his wife. This joy will be short-lived, since he is leaving us to take part in this war, into which we have been drawn God knows how or why. Not only with you, at the center of affairs and of the world, but here too, amid these rural labors and this stillness which townspeople usually imagine to reign in the country, the echoes of war are heard and make themselves painfully felt. My father talks of nothing but marches and countermarches, of which I understand nothing, and the day before yesterday, taking my usual walk through the village street, I witnessed a heartrending scene. It was a party of recruits, levied among us and being sent off to the army. One should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of those who were leaving, and heard the sobbing on both sides! One would think that mankind had forgotten the laws of our Divine Saviour, who taught us love and forgiveness of injuries, and that it placed its highest merit in the art of killing one another. Farewell, dear and good friend. May our Divine Saviour and His Most Holy Mother keep you under their holy and mighty protection. Marie."

The field marshal, leaving this occupation to us, watches us and waits for envelopes addressed to himself. We search, but none are to be found. The field marshal grows uneasy, sets to work himself, and finds letters from the sovereign to Count T., to Prince V., and to others. He flies into the most violent rage, loses all self-control, seizes the letters, opens them, and reads those addressed to others... And writes his famous order to Count Bennigsen. The field marshal is angry with the sovereign, and punishes all of us: it is perfectly logical! Such is the first act of the comedy. In those that follow, the interest and the drollery naturally increase. After the field marshal’s departure it turns out that we are in sight of the enemy, and that a battle must be given. Buxhövden is commander-in-chief by seniority, but General Bennigsen is by no means of that opinion, especially as he, with his own corps, is in sight of the enemy and wishes to seize the chance of a battle. So he gives one. This is the battle of Pultusk, which is reckoned a great victory, but which, in my opinion, is nothing of the kind. We civilians have, as you know, a very bad habit of deciding whether a battle is won or lost. He who has retreated after a battle has lost it, that is what we say, and judging by that we lost the battle of Pultusk. In a word, we retreat after the battle, but send a courier to Petersburg with news of a victory, and General Bennigsen does not yield the command of the army to General Buxhövden, hoping to receive from Petersburg, in gratitude for his victory, the title of commander-in-chief. During this interregnum we begin a very original and interesting series of maneuvers. Our plan no longer consists, as it ought to, in avoiding or attacking the enemy, but only in avoiding General Buxhövden, who by right of seniority ought to be our chief. We pursue this object with such energy that, even in crossing a river with no fords, we burn the bridge, with the aim of putting distance between ourselves and our enemy, who at the present moment is not Bonaparte but Buxhövden. General Buxhövden very nearly was attacked and captured by superior enemy forces, in consequence of one of these very maneuvers that were saving us from him. Buxhövden pursues us—we flee. No sooner has he crossed to one side of the river than we cross again to the other. At last our enemy Buxhövden catches us and attacks. An explanation follows. Both generals lose their tempers, and the matter very nearly comes to a duel between the two commanders-in-chief. But fortunately, at the most critical moment, the courier who carried to Petersburg the news of the victory at Pultusk returns and brings us the appointment of a commander-in-chief, and our first enemy—Buxhövden—is vanquished. We can now turn our thoughts to the second enemy—Bonaparte. But it turns out that at this very moment a third enemy rises up before us—the Orthodox soldiery—who with loud outcries demand bread, beef, biscuit, hay, oats, and heaven knows what besides! The stores are empty, the roads are impassable. The Orthodox soldiery begin to plunder, and the plundering reaches such a pitch that the last campaign could not give you the faintest notion of it. Half the regiments form themselves into free bands that roam the country and put everything to fire and sword. The inhabitants are utterly ruined, the hospitals are crammed with the sick, and there is famine everywhere. Twice the marauders even attacked headquarters itself, and the commander-in-chief was obliged to call out a battalion of soldiers to drive them off. In one of these attacks they carried off my empty trunk and my dressing gown.
